Extend a Set of Cohort Labels

Source: R/cohort_extend.R
cohort_extend.Rd

Add new equal-width cohort labels to the end of an existing set.

Usage

cohort_extend(
  labels,
  n = 1L,
  width = NULL,
  include_labels = TRUE,
  interpret_single = c("lower", "upper"),
  interpret_multi = NULL,
  interpret_fail = c("error", "warn", "silent")
)

Arguments

labels

Vector of cohort labels.

n

Number of cohorts to add. Default is 1.

width

Width of the cohorts to be added.

include_labels

Should the return value include labels? Default is TRUE.

interpret_single

How to interpret a label for a single year, such as "2020". Choices are "lower" (the default) and "upper". See below for details.

interpret_multi

How to interpret a label that refers to multiple years, such as "2020-2025". Choices are NULL (the default), "at_upper", and "below_upper". See below for details.

interpret_fail

Action if element of labels cannot be interpreted. Choices are "error" (the default), "warn", and "silent".

Value

A factor if labels is a factor, and a character vector otherwise. If labels is a factor, the new cohorts are added as levels, after the existing levels.

Details

The new cohorts start at the highest upper limit of the cohorts in labels, including unused levels if labels is a factor. By default, the width of the new cohorts is the width of the cohort with the highest upper limit, but a value can be specified through the width argument.

labels cannot include totals, missing values, or cohorts that are open on the right.

Rules for interpreting inputs

Single-year

Labels for single-year cohorts sometimes refer to the lower limits of cohorts, and sometimes refer to upper limits. For instance, the label "2020" is sometimes used to refer to the cohort that starts at midnight on 1 January 2020 and ends at midnight on 1 January 2021, and is sometimes used to refer to the cohort that starts at midnight on 1 July 2019 and ends at midnight on 1 July 2020.

The interpret_single argument can be used to distinguish between the two conventions:

interpret_singleRuleExample
"lower""a" -> [a,a+1)"2020" -> [2020,2021)
"upper""a" -> [a-1,a)"2020" -> [2019,2020)

Multi-year

In labels for multi-year cohorts, the second number is sometimes the upper limit of the cohort, and sometimes the upper limit minus 1. For instance, the cohort that starts at midnight on 1 January 2020 and ends at midnight on 1 January 2025 is sometimes labelled "2020-2025" and is sometimes labelled "2020-2024".

The interpret_multi argument can be used to distinguish between the two conventions:

interpret_multiRuleExample
"at_upper""a-b" -> [a,b)"2020-2025" -> [2020,2025)
"below_upper""a-b" -> [a,b+1)"2020-2024" -> [2020,2025)

If interpret_multi is NULL (the default), then multi-year labels are interpreted using the "at_upper" convention. If, however, the "at_upper" convention leads to intervals with widths 4, 9, 14, ..., then agetime emits a message. Supplying an explicit value for interpret_multi silences this message.

Open

A cohort that is open on the left has no lower limit, and a cohort that is open on the right has no upper limit. Labels for open cohorts are not affected by interpret_single or interpret_multi.

Some examples of open cohorts:

LabelInterval
"<2000", "before 2000", "under 2000"(-Inf,2000)
"2000 or earlier", "up to 2000"(-Inf,2001)
"2000+", "2000 or more", "2000 or later"[2000,Inf)

Labels starting with "-", such as "-2000", are not accepted.

See also

  • age_extend() Age equivalent of cohort_extend()

  • period_extend() Period equivalent of cohort_extend()

Examples

labels <- c("2020-2025", "2025-2030")
cohort_extend(labels, n = 2)
#> [1] "2020-2025" "2025-2030" "2030-2035" "2035-2040"
cohort_extend(labels, n = 2, width = 10)
#> [1] "2020-2025" "2025-2030" "2030-2040" "2040-2050"
cohort_extend(labels, n = 2, include_labels = FALSE)
#> [1] "2030-2035" "2035-2040"
